notes.title: Luzon commerce and maritime connections
notes.body: Tomé Pires composed the Suma Oriental in 1512–1515, drawing on commercial information from others. It describes Luzon traders and regional links involving Borneo and Malacca. This is evidence of a wider commercial setting, not a record of Ache's dealings or a verified route for Mulaw. The original Portuguese passage has not been collated for this chapter.

notes.title: Exchange and local political relationships
notes.body: Laura Lee Junker's Raiding, Trading, and Feasting (1999) analyzes the political importance of exchange in Philippine chiefdoms. It supports asking how access, obligations and reputation could interact; it does not document the particular landing arrangements or prices here.

notes.title: Fictional reconstruction and later testimony
notes.body: Sera, Lana, Raya, Dala, the basket maker, the wax shipment, the repaired step, and the disputed bamboo tally are invented. The negotiations are not attested customs or recorded agreements. Later sixteenth-century Spanish accounts of Tagalog obligations cannot establish the precise rules of an earlier Maynila landing. Mulaw is a fictional acquaintance from Book I Chapter 7 who offered a name and advice, never a pledged boat or alliance; no reunion occurs in this chapter.
